title: The Peloponnese and the Ionian Islands: the dialects closest to the standard
lead: For more than a century, Greeks were taught that their national language was 'based on Peloponnesian'. It is easy to see why: Peloponnesian and Ionian speech sound closer to Standard Modern Greek than any other dialect, the Peloponnese was the heart of the 1821 revolution, and the Ionian poets created modern Greek literature. But recent research has turned the story around. The Peloponnese has plenty of its own features (**πάω το χωριό**, **ήγλεπα**, **ομορφύτερος**), and much of its similarity to the standard may be the result of its speakers converging on Athenian usage, not the other way round. The Ionian Islands, never ruled by the Ottomans, have a Venetian accent of their own.
facts: Peloponnese (except Tsakonia and Mani); the Ionian Islands Corfu, Paxoi, Kefalonia, Ithaca and Zakynthos; western Epirus. **Lefkada** has northern vowels and belongs with Central Greece.
Trudgill's **central** group: Peloponnese, Ionian Islands and western Epirus.
The 14th-century «Χρονικό του Μορέως», in vernacular Greek; the Ionian School of poetry, 19th century.

Peloponnese: Frankish, Byzantine, Ottoman (1460), Venetian (1685–1715), Ottoman again until 1821. Ionian Islands: Venetian for up to four centuries, then French, Russian–Ottoman, British (1815–1864); union with Greece 1864.
Strongly influenced by the standard; features survive in villages and in local accents, for example in Patras.

sections.h: The Peloponnese: from the Morea to the new state

timeline.text: Slavic tribes settle much of the Peloponnese. Byzantium re-Hellenises the region; Slavic place names remain (Αράχωβα, Βελιγοστή).
The Frankish **Principality of Achaea**. The «Χρονικό του Μορέως» tells its story in everyday Greek, full of French words.
The Byzantine **Despotate of the Morea** at Mystras, a last centre of Byzantine learning.
Albanian-speaking (Arvanite) settlers arrive in large numbers in Argolis, Corinthia and elsewhere.
The Revolution starts in the Peloponnese. Nafplio is the first capital of Greece (1829–1834); Peloponnesians move to the new capital Athens in large numbers.

sections.h: Did Peloponnesian really become Standard Greek?
sections.text: The traditional view, found in Mackridge, Browning and Kontosopoulos, is that the standard grew out of Peloponnesian and Ionian speech. Nikolaos Pantelidis and others now argue that this view rested more on history than on linguistic data: the Peloponnese led the Revolution, and Peloponnesians flooded into Athens. When the dialect material is studied closely, it shows many differences from the standard. The striking similarities may come from **convergence**: Peloponnesians were the first rural Greeks to adopt the new common language of Athens, and they did so early and thoroughly. Whether there was ever a single 'Peloponnesian koine' is unknown. See the **History** page for how the standard actually formed, from a mix of urban Athenian speech, Peloponnesian and Ionian input, and the refugee speech of the 19th and 20th centuries.

sections.after: Even in a big city close to Athens the dialect is not gone: in Patras, Dimitris Papazachariou found several non-standard pronunciations of **λ**, used differently according to speakers' origin, gender and education.

sections.after: Several of these, such as **τρανύτερος**, **λέγανε** and **όντας**, are also heard in Athens, because Peloponnesians were so many of its 19th-century settlers.

sections.h: The Ionian Islands: Greek under Venice

timeline.text: Corfu under Venice; Zakynthos from 1485, Kefalonia and Ithaca from 1500, Lefkada from 1684. Italian is the language of the nobility and administration; the islands are the only part of Greece the Ottomans never held for long.
After the fall of Candia, Cretan refugees bring the literature of the Cretan Renaissance to the islands.
French rule, then the **Septinsular Republic** (1800–1807), the first autonomous Greek state of modern times.
British protectorate. The **Ionian Academy** in Corfu (1824) is the first Greek university.
The **Ionian School** of poets (Solomos, Kalvos, later Valaoritis and Mavilis) proves that spoken Greek can carry great poetry.

sections.text: The most recognisable Ionian feature is not a vowel or a consonant but the **intonation**, the sing-song melody of Corfu and Zakynthos. The vowels are southern and close to the standard.

sample.h: «Ύμνος εις την Ελευθερίαν», by Dionysios Solomos
sample.intro: Written on Zakynthos in 1823; its first stanzas became the Greek national anthem. Solomos, raised speaking Italian, chose the spoken Greek of his island for his poetry. Public domain.
lines: που με βιά μετράει τη γη.
en: I know you by the terrible edge
I know you by the look
with which you swiftly measure the earth.
and brave as you were before,
sample.source: Διονύσιος Σολωμός, «Ύμνος εις την Ελευθερίαν» (1823), stanzas 1–2.

culture.text: The Venetian legacy is still audible in the Ionian **καντάδες**, serenades sung in harmony to guitar and mandolin, and in the philharmonic brass bands of Corfu, which play at every Easter procession. On Corfu, people still use dozens of Italian words in daily life. In the Peloponnese, Kalamata's **καλαματιανός** is the dance that every Greek wedding plays.

questions.q: What do many linguists now think about Peloponnesian as the 'basis' of Standard Greek?
options: The similarity may come from Peloponnesian converging on Athenian usage

questions.why: Pantelidis and others argue that the influence may have run from the standard to the dialect.
Peloponnesian uses a bare accusative for destination.
Feminines in -α can form the genitive in **-ός**: νυχτός, μερός.
